extracted.intended_audience: middle- and upper-class women, parents, and general readers seeking advice on social etiquette, personal conduct, and hygiene
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance on honesty, social conventionalities, intimate boundaries, child-rearing of manners, table and visiting etiquette, and personal hygiene/stomach care for householders and social persons. Emphasis is on cultivating durable 'polish' (finish) rather than superficial affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veracity / truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid intentional falsehood; truthfulness is a moral duty and a virtue to cultivate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses the technical definition of a lie as 'something told with the intention to deceive' and laments that few people are perfectly truthful. Urges cultivating veracity as essential for the 'integrity of the soul' and for preserving children's confidence. Advises pruning loose statements and preferring understatement rather than magnification when telling a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of gratuitous frankness
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not confuse 'being frank' (saying just what one thinks) with truthfulness — gratuitous, unkind criticism is impertinence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a 'frank friend' tells you your gown does not fit or criticizes your household management without being asked, this is an unwarrantable liberty. One may be truthful without bestowing unsolicited and hurtful remarks; such speech often stems from disagreeable temper rather than moral high-mindedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exaggeration and sensationalizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from supplying imagined details to fill gaps in overheard or partial information; do not let imagination turn scraps into sensational falsehoods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by an anecdote where a girl overhears bits of a conversation and 'allows a vivid imagination to supply the portions she did not hear,' producing a garbled, sensational story. Warns that many 'romances' and exaggerated accounts arise from this impulse to produce sensation; encourages cutting down rather than magnifying a story ('A couple of ciphers less are better than one too many').

rubrics_metrics.name: Set a truth-telling example for children
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents and elders must be absolutely truthful in word and deed to prevent hereditary or learned deceit in children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that the habit of lying is often transmitted in families and that children notice and remember adult exaggerations or untruthfulness, losing trust. Recommends strict self-guard over speech, correcting one's own lapses, and cultivating veracity as a vital necessity. 'When your child... once discovers in you exaggeration or untruthfulness, he remembers it always.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe conventionalities (the 'Gospel of Conventionalities')
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventional social practices and small 'make-believes' perform valuable social functions and beautify life; they should be observed rather than scorned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Harriet Beecher Stowe's idea that women 'make life beautiful' by keeping up conventions. Argues that many conventions have hygienic or utilitarian reasons or serve the greatest good. Rejects the view that all conventions are mere sham; they maintain social order and comfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate polish and durable 'finish' rather than superficial varnish
rubrics_metrics.description: Refinement should be genuine and ingrained; superficial polish that flakes under stress reveals poor breeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the wagon-builder metaphor: finish (smooth, well-varnished surface) makes a carriage look costly, but the underlying wood must be sound or the varnish will flake. Likewise, social polish must be durable; intimacy should not allow familiarity that reveals lack of true refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect precedence and basic drawing-room protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon entering a hostess's drawing-room, seek out and pay respects to the hostess first before speaking to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is improper to enter a lady's parlor and stop to talk with someone before finding and addressing the hostess. If addressed while searching for the lady, make a brief apology and pass on until you have found her. This small token of respect is part of good breeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ring or knock before entering a friend's house or private room
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not enter a friend's house without ringing the bell, nor enter private rooms (bedroom/sanctum) without knocking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even intimate friends should not presume on being allowed to enter unannounced. Housekeepers may be engaged in tasks and wish a moment to compose themselves. The bedroom should be so completely one's own that nearest relations are expected to knock before entering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not offer unsolicited advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless your opinion is requested, refrain from giving advice about others' affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unsolicited advice is a form of intrusion; a safe rule is to decline to give judgments unless asked (the author jokes that lawyers charge high fees because they decline to advise unless consulted). Giving unsolicited advice often implicates one unnecessarily in others' business and is thankless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not correct another's child in the parent's presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid reprimanding or disciplining someone else's child in front of the child's parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such intervention is a gross breach of finish and can anger the child's parents. Examples: visitor reproving 'Johnny' in presence of his mother or adding severe remarks that undermine parental authority and annoy both parent and child.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain appropriate boundaries of familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Familiarity must not transgress decency: do not touch a woman on arm/shoulder to attract attention, avoid physical familiarity, and do not presume on first-name terms without consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of unacceptable familiarity include slapping a woman on the back, squeezing her arm, or holding her hand longer than friendship dictates. If a man asks to be called by his first name and the friendship justifies it, respond accordingly — but a 'finished' person will not assume the right to drop honorifics unbidden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious before deepening friendship to intimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the friendship is desired before moving beyond acquaintance or familiar friend to intimate terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: 'Be certain that your friendship is desired before going more than halfway.' Anecdotal remark: 'She is certainly my familiar friend. We can never be intimate.' — do not force intimacy on another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid discussing family faults or private domestic matters with outsiders
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not 'wash your dirty linen in public'; keep domestic complaints and family shortcomings within the family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if your father, mother, brother or husband have faults, as long as you pretend to be on speaking terms with them, 'stand up for them against all the rest of the world.' Public complaining about family is discourteous and betrays lack of loyalty and breeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train children early in small courtesies
rubrics_metrics.description: Mothers/guardians are responsible for beginning early and persistently to train children in manners and small courtesies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First impressions are lasting; teach children 'the small sweet courtesies of life' in nursery and family life so they grow into well-bred persons. Correct tricks of manner (touching a lady, consulting watch in company, glancing at addresses) before they are confirmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid intrusive questions about finances and private expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from asking acquaintances about amounts paid for purchases, income, rent, mortgage, or household costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists examples of impertinent queries: 'How much did you pay for that horse?' 'Was that gown very expensive?' 'What rent do you pay?' Such questions tempt the target to lose composure and are socially improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table etiquette and small tokens of good breeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe accepted table manners and small tokens (e.g., resigning chair to a lady, proper serving order); perform post-visit courtesies like the 'bread-and-butter' thank-you note promptly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the 'bread-and-butter letter' — a brief note written soon after a visit informing hostess of safe arrival and thanking her. Cites examples of failures of etiquette (asking a butler for milk, requesting mustard at table) as signs of neglected upbringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cautious forms of reference to people (handles and names)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'finished' person does not speak of a lady to strangers without the 'handle' (title). Avoid referring to people by last names only in casual speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saying only 'Smith' or 'Brown' without courtesy titles is a sign that 'the last coat of varnish was neglected.' Use appropriate modes of address in speaking of others to preserve decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate physical cleanliness and skin care to support health
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the skin and pores clean to dispose of effete matter and maintain health; use soap and warm water daily and open pores by baths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that the skin's pores act as drains for impurities and must be kept open. Recommend free use of soap and warm water, sponging once a day in perspiring people, and frequent plunge baths to open pores and thoroughly cleanse the surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care of the stomach: prevention, moderate remedies, and diet
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent digestive disorder by careful diet and habits; soothe rather than punish an irritated stomach; use fasting and light food rather than immediate dosing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: a few hours' fasting may be excellent; when eating, do so slowly and take light food (milk-toast, hot beef-tea). Avoid foods that disagree (hot breads, pastry, fried/greasy food, nuts, many sweets) and do not become dependent on medicines to ward off indigestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overuse and dependency on over-the-counter remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely habitually on bicarbonate of soda, pepsin tablets, or patent medicines; such dependence can cause harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that frequent large doses of bicarbonate have in some cases produced cancerous conditions of the stomach lining; warns against degeneration into an incurable habit of depending on remedies after every meal. Advocates dietary care over routine dosing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise regularly and keep bodily 'drains' functioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular and abundant exercise is necessary along with hygiene to maintain health and proper digestion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions exercise as a 'desideratum' following the discussion of bathing and skin care; frames it as part of the preventive hygiene regimen to keep the body's elimination and general health in working order.
